utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Good morning to everyone in and just outside this courtroom. Would you please call the case, Madam Registrar.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Case Number IT-98-29-T, the Prosecutor versus Stanislav Galic.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Thank you very much. The Defence started to cross-examine the witness yesterday. You're ready to resume?

utterances.speaker: MR. PILETTA-ZANIN
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, Mr. President. However, before we do so, the Defence deems that it is necessary to make the following commentary and to raise some issues with regards to the conduct of the procedure and with regards to the evidence. The Defence deems it necessary to do so at this present moment for the simple reason that the way the documents are communicated is definitely a handicap and it is a violation of essential rights reserved to the Defence in order to conduct a fair trial.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Please proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. PILETTA-ZANIN
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you. Mr. President, Your Honours, thank you for handing us the floor. You have indicated to us yesterday that it would be good that if we have a problem with regards to the reading, the legibility of the documents, that is communicated to us by the Prosecution, to inform your Chamber within 48 hours. We shall attempt, try, to follow that rule, although it is not always possible to see where the problem is when we have 40.000 documents. It is not always easy to see where the problem will be. We can't always know ahead of time if a document is not well photocopied or if it is badly translated. This being said, Mr. President, Your Honours, we would like to draw the attention of your Chamber to three documents. I will first talk about a mail, a letter, that we had sent on the 25th of July, 2001. When I say that we have sent this letter, I am talking about the Defence, of course, because your humble servant, myself, was not working this case yet. So it was a letter sent to my honourable colleague, Mr. Mark Ierace. There was an annex to this letter and it was four pages representing lists. I do have copies of these lists and I will hand them to you. Those were lists of documents that the Defence were deeming not to be enough legible. I will first read on the last page, on page 7 of this concerning the item, illegible documentation. It is written in English. The following document: 0026-8535, 20026-8586. Those are very precisely these documents that we have examined yesterday, the certificates which were subjected to, most likely, some kind of scratching of the date. So we have seen that it was not very legible, and we can see that it says that this has not been addressed, this problem has not been addressed at the time. We have reiterated on many occasions, and we have asked the Prosecution to hand out, to hand us, to communicate to us, very clear copies. We have done it on the 8th of October, 2001, by sending them a letter. I will also hand you and show you this document so that you may take possession of it, read it, and in this letter, we have underlined all the problems linked to the quality of the material that we receive. Some motions were then submitted with regards to military documents, for instance. It was said that these orders and that these instructions, these military documents, would be sent to us and put to us in our mailbox. It is the mailbox that the Defence has here in this Tribunal. We are talking about the 8th of October. At the time, we were talking about a delay of a few days, 12th of October, 2001, and you have only -- you have seen that only last week have we received one-third of this documentation, or actually we were told that it can be handed out, delivered, and it was done, and I thank the Prosecution. But it was only in the month of April 2002. And after that -- or rather, only after that we have cross-examined witnesses. On the 4th of January, 2002, Mr. President, I intervened once again, and when I say "I," I mean the Defence. The Defence asked once again the Prosecution the following: We were telling them since the medical documents are illegible and that even some documents are not included, I thank you, of wanting to submit to you, but we cannot accept them. So we have reiterated this on many occasions. We have asked the Prosecution on many occasions. Maybe I would like Mr. Stamp to intervene at this point. Or maybe I should let Mr. Stamp, rather, answer.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: I understand that this correspondence is not directly dealing with documents we could expect today or tomorrow or the day after tomorrow?

utterances.speaker: MR. PILETTA-ZANIN
utterances.text: [Interpretation] It corresponds to those documents. It also corresponds to some other documents, but it's basically with regards to these documents. If I may continue, Mr. President. In the month of December, 2001, your humble servant asked for a meeting between the Defence and the Prosecution to say the following: That given this very bad quality of copies, documents, we have noticed, and you will certainly remember because I did raise the issue before this Chamber, the search engines or this way -- the search system was not effective, and I tried to -- I attempted to show your Chamber that we should maybe look and search differently. But the problem was not there. The problem was with regards to the quality of the copies that we get, the documents. And the Prosecution told us that what they should do is to communicate to us hard copies, paper copies, and that for the rest, for all the other, computer support was only an additional support, that they were not -- it was not necessary for them to hand it to us. So we were only talking therefore about hard copies, about paper copies. But what is the reality of the fact? And it is the following: That since 1991, as of the beginning of this year, we have been asking clear copies that are legible and available. It was refused to us, and you have seen the quality of the documents that we have received. The following question is asked -- is raised, therefore, in law, and it is the following: Is the Prosecution -- has the Prosecution fulfilled its obligation with regards to Article 65 ter, 65(f), I believe, to communicate at least six months before the opening of the trial documents on which they wish to base their Defence. We have -- or the Prosecution, rather. We have a computer system that cannot work. And when we have documents, when we receive documents that are in such poor quality, and you have seen it yesterday; we have called it a "black box" often here in this trial. I believe that the logical deduction is the following: By delivering what they knew being a black box at the time, the Prosecution was not fulfilling his obligation, that is, to deliver, to submit the documents in question. And he was doing it fully knowing that they had legible documents within their possession and which is something that we were able to see now, yesterday. Since we have documents that are perfectly legible that were submitted yesterday by the Prosecution, whereas the documents that the Defence had received at the time was completely illegible. We, therefore, ask that these documents should not be considered as being documents that are disclosed on the regular basis to the Defence, and this is why we deem that all these documents should be excluded, therefore, not be admitted as evidence. Mr. President, this is a formal conclusion on our behalf, and to support this, I will hand the usher copies. We also have some copies for the Prosecution, and we are talking about something that happened a long time ago. Therefore, we shall hand them the three correspondences, these three letters that I have handed to them, and I must say that these letters have not received an answer. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Stamp, would you like to respond now or -- ?

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: Briefly, just to say, (a), when it comes to medical documentation and what the Defence has referred to specifically, we did everything, perhaps more than even necessary, to send various missions to various places to try to obtain the best copies available. We invited the Defence to have a look at the copies that are in our vaults because some of the documents could not be photocopied or were not photocopied in an ideal -- with the legibility being ideal. That is all I would like to say at this moment. My friend, in this submission, as it were, has referred to a history and to a variety of letters which he has sent. And he has said that we have never answered. He has said that we have refused to give them legible copies. There are documents relevant to this submission. It would be impossible for me to answer without having a look at all the documents relevant to what he has said, and to give the Court a precise answer, to assist the Court in coming to an assessment of this submission which my friend has raised this morning. So if I could perhaps be given some time to look into some of the specific allegations or statements that he has made and to respond to it, I'd be very grateful.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Stamp, I'll give you some time. But that doesn't keep me off from making observations: The first is that sometimes the documents in your possession are badly legible as such. By copying, you can't make them any better legible than they are. Nevertheless, yesterday, we got the impression that, by copying, you can make them less legible. And we could expect from both parties that if they provide the other party with copies, that the copy should not be less legible than the documents in the hands of the other party. And at least we got a clear indication yesterday that that is what has happened, and that shouldn't happen, of course. You can't make them any better as they are, but you can make them worse, and I would say that is not acceptable. The second issue I'd like to make an observation about is that, if there are complaints about the legibility of documents, in writing, I expect parties to respond to that. I don't know whether it has been done or not. It has now been alleged that you did not respond. If that's true, that's not the way it should be done. The third observation I'd like to make is that as has been stressed by you yesterday, Mr. Stamp, and that if the Defence finds that the copies as they are provided are unsatisfactory, that of course your last resort is to inspection of the documents in the hands of the Prosecution. That could finally perhaps not solve the problem, but at least clarify whether there are any better legible copies. And the fourth observation I'd like to make is that if there's a disclosure obligation, if it's not fulfilled, that it's not an automatic consequence that all documents not disclosed in -- either in proper time or in proper quality, will have to be excluded. The Chamber will have to decide on what the legal consequences will be of any failure or temporary failure to fulfill disclosure obligations. It could, for example, be that extra time should be granted to one of the parties to be better able to prepare for the presentation of their case after they have had an opportunity to inspect the documents or the copies of these documents. These are just some general observations I'd like to make. We would like to hear from the Prosecution in response to the specific correspondence given to the Chamber by the Defence. If one of the documents appearing in this correspondence turns up today or tomorrow, the day after tomorrow, would you please then indicate that clearly so that we do not wait, so that we know that it has become urgent at this very moment. Otherwise, I would say that within one or two days, Mr. Stamp, I expect that the Prosecution will be able to give a response to the submissions made by the Defence. Then, if there's another issue at this moment, then I'd like to hear it.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: No other issue. Before I sit down, before the cross-examination resumes, may I indicate that we will respond to every issue that the Court has raised, as fully as we can.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: However, in respect to the inspection, may I just announce through the Court that we have invited the Defence to inspect on many occasions, and the invitation is still open. I know the Court is not sitting on Friday, so perhaps the Defence would like to use that opportunity, or perhaps in the afternoons. Through the Court, I again invite the Defence to inspect whatever documents that we have which they are not satisfied of the legibility of the copies. It is just an invitation. Thanks, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. PILETTA-ZANIN
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, Mr. President. Two observations: Firstly, we will have to, in fact, inspect some of the documents which I mentioned earlier, which are partly found in this correspondence, and we have received clear indications yesterday here that they are underlined in blue on the last page of the correspondence of July 2001. And the second point which seems essential to be raised is the following, is I am waiting once again. And what I am waiting for is that before I am able to be efficient and to cross-examine this witness, I am waiting for Mr. Stamp to answer to the following question: How is it possible that they may have incurred some scratchings on these documents or that one attempted to perhaps cross out some dates. So this information seems to be extremely useful before I begin the cross-examination.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Could you give any indication, Mr. Stamp, I mean, whether it's formally introduced or not, to respond to the question of -- well, we noticed yesterday that there seemed to be entries of other dates in these documents. Have you any -- could you give Mr. Piletta-Zanin any clue on what could explain? I don't know, it's not a formal explanation.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: Mr. President, I would not like to comment on that without having precise knowledge. The documents are the best representation of what we have in our evidence vault. They are free to inspect it. The issue was raised, and the Court expressed some concern. It is our position as prosecutors, indeed, our duty to try to proceed in a manner which will please the Court. And therefore, we have undertaken to give precise answers. It might well mean that we will have to call more witnesses than we intend, to explain certain things. But the issue, having been raised by the Defence, we will do what is necessary to clarify it. I cannot, however, see how it is that the cross-examination of my learned friend might be hampered in respect to a witness who did not make these documents. The witness did not make these documents. The witness can only say these are the documents. These documents were signed by Dr. Dobraca. The issue has been raised and we will do whatever necessary to clarify it. I would not want to speculate an answer at this moment, if it pleases you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Piletta-Zanin, I think what could be expected from the Defence at this moment is to conduct its cross-examination as far as possible. But I am fully aware, and this Chamber is fully aware - we discussed the matter - that a lot of questions are still there. And if at a later stage it would become relevant to recall this witness because of what then has become clear, which is unclear now, then of course the Defence should have an opportunity to do so. On the other hand, this is not a free -- this is not to say that under whatever circumstances, the witness could be recalled in order to resume any cross-examination. But as I indicated, that if that would become relevant on the basis of what we learn later on on these documents, so that you're not able to cross-examine on these relevant aspects the witness, of course the Defence should have an opportunity to recall that witness. But, for example, if it's cross-examination on parts of the documents that are fairly legible or other kind of information, then, of course, that would be different. You might have noticed that this Chamber is not very happy to receive documents, to see documents on which we find clear indications that there have been multiple entries on certain questions, and I'm specifically referring to the lines 2 and 3 of the form which was used. I'll now give you the opportunity, after having said this, to resume the cross-examination of the witness, unless there's any specific remark you'd like to make.

utterances.speaker: MR. PILETTA-ZANIN
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I'm terribly sorry. I thank the Chamber for this observation. The Chamber will have noted the Defence was not particularly happy to receive these documents as well. But this being said, I have two observations, the first being the following: We know very well, Mr. President, that when one cross-examines or examines a witness, something called current might be -- might exist. When we call it current, by this I mean that when the witness comes back, the witness might prepare himself in a different way, and the circumstances are different in which this witness is recalled. And whatever he may say at that time, the truth, truth will not be said the same way, will not be given under the same circumstances as it was given during the -- his first examination. So if the Defence proceeds this way and if they hand us documents that are "scratched out," one must say that the Defence was handicapped by this. And the second point that I wish to raise is the issue of a translation. We have examined during the night various translations, and it is true to say that these translations correspond to a form. They are mechanical, if you will. But it appears that these translations have three problematic issues, if you will. The first is the title and the nature of the document. In English, it is defined as being a post-mortem record. I am not quite certain that the description given of this document in Serbian is the same thing. The two titles in Serbian and in English do not correspond. And the second issue is that apparently on the translation, we would see, and I say "would see" because, of course, we all lose our Latin, if you will. We are all lost. We seem to see two signatures. On the translations, we can see the appearance of two signatures: Firstly, the first one being the one belonging to the head of the service, the institution, the institute for forensic medicine, and the second one is the doctor whose name was mentioned on a few occasions. This is one observation. And the last observation that I wish to raise, Mr. President, is that you have deciphered very clearly 80 per cent of the stamp that was in the original documents, whereas in the translation, we see the following signature and stamp of the institute, whereas the stamp which appears on the original document is not the stamp of the institute. It is the stamp of the university, the medical faculty of Sarajevo, but it is not a stamp belonging to the forensic institute. We are, therefore, worried, and once again we reiterate that there is probably a translation problem. It is not another document with another stamp that was given to the translation department. Those are documents that were written in January of 1995. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Thank you for your observations, Mr. Piletta-Zanin. Let me first respond to the latter part. It's quite clear that if an interpreter indicates that it's the stamp of the institute, of course, that's an interpretation but not a linguistic interpretation but just an interpretation of what the stamp is. It's not a matter of translation as such. Then you said that the Defence is handicapped in cross-examining the witness and would be handicapped if the witness would be recalled. I think this Chamber is fully aware of that problem, and that even a lapse of time could influence the -- and even to some extent handicap the Defence. If I can say it in general words, life is not without handicaps. It is not a matter of whether you are handicapped, but it's a matter of whether it would make this trial an unfair trial. I think that's what's always, not in the back of our minds but even in the front of our minds. So we'll -- we are fully aware of that problem, and of course we'll have to assess what it actually means for the Defence under these circumstances. Then, could you resume the cross-examination of the witness.

utterances.speaker: MR. PILETTA-ZANIN
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I would gladly do so, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Usher, would you --

utterances.speaker: MR. PILETTA-ZANIN
utterances.text: [Interpretation] But I believe that my friend, Ms. Pilipovic, will continue, will resume, and I may have maybe some questions at some point.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Please be seated, Mr. Suljic. I'd first like to apologise that we kept you waiting for 40 minutes. We had to deal with some procedural issues so that caused the delay. Then, may I remind that you're still bound by the solemn declaration you gave yesterday. Now Ms. Pilipovic will resume the cross-examination. Please proceed, Ms. Pilipovic.

utterances.speaker: MS. PILIPOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Good morning, Mr. Suljic.

utterances.speaker: EDIN SULJIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Good morning.

utterances.speaker: MS. PILIPOVIC
utterances.text: Yesterday, we discontinued our examination at the point where you told us that you had arrived at the Markale market with your team. You also told us that some UN observers were also there. Is that correct?

utterances.speaker: EDIN SULJIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. PILIPOVIC
utterances.text: Can you please confirm for us that there were stalls at the Markale market that were undamaged and that the goods that were on these stalls were not scattered around?

utterances.speaker: EDIN SULJIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I cannot confirm that.

utterances.speaker: MS. PILIPOVIC
utterances.text: As far as you remember, were there any such stalls there?

utterances.speaker: EDIN SULJIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't remember.

utterances.speaker: MS. PILIPOVIC
utterances.text: Can you please tell us who in your team was the first to notice the flight stabiliser, the tail-fin, rather?

utterances.speaker: EDIN SULJIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I'm not quite sure. It may have been the crime scene technician, but I'm not sure so I can't really answer your question.

utterances.speaker: MS. PILIPOVIC
utterances.text: Were you personally present at the site where the tail-fin was located?

utterances.speaker: EDIN SULJIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. PILIPOVIC
utterances.text: Before the location of the tail-fin was identified, did anyone clear the area where the tail-fin was?

utterances.speaker: EDIN SULJIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MS. PILIPOVIC
utterances.text: Can you please describe to us the area on the market where the tail-fin was.

utterances.speaker: EDIN SULJIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: The market was strewn with goods and other items that were sold there. There was quite a lot of blood and human body parts. The tail-fin of the projectile was located in front of one of the stalls. It was buried into the asphalt and concrete surface. Around the tail-fin itself, there were some other items scattered around.

utterances.speaker: MS. PILIPOVIC
utterances.text: Did any members of your team clear the ground around the area where the tail-fin was? I think I already asked you that question, but do you remember?

utterances.speaker: EDIN SULJIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: When the tail-fin was found, the area around it was cleared, as that would make it possible to determine on the basis of the imprint of the shrapnel, the shell shrapnel, the direction from which the projectile had come, and other elements important for the ballistics experts and the crime scene technician.

utterances.speaker: MS. PILIPOVIC
utterances.text: Can you please tell us who pulled out the tail-fin?

utterances.speaker: EDIN SULJIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Since the UN members also attended, were present at the investigation, I would think that the tail-fin was pulled out by one of the UN members.

utterances.speaker: MS. PILIPOVIC
utterances.text: Was this moment when the tail-fin was pulled out photographed or filmed in any way? Can you please tell us that?

utterances.speaker: EDIN SULJIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I'm not quite sure, but I do believe that it was.

utterances.speaker: MS. PILIPOVIC
utterances.text: Could you please confirm whether there were any shrapnel at the Markale market?

utterances.speaker: EDIN SULJIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. PILIPOVIC
utterances.text: Can you please tell us whether any members of your team picked up the shrapnel, the fragments?

utterances.speaker: EDIN SULJIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: The fragments were gathered in the shops that were in the vicinity. The fragments had entered the shops through glass windows and doors, and also some were pulled out from the facades, just as the shrapnel that were found there on the actual market.

utterances.speaker: MS. PILIPOVIC
utterances.text: Could you please tell us who took the tail-fin, if it was taken anywhere, and where it was taken to and what about the shell shrapnel? Were they also taken somewhere, and do you have any knowledge as to where they are now?

utterances.speaker: EDIN SULJIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: The tail-fin and the shrapnel were handed over for further processing to the crime scene technicians. And after the processing, they were submitted together with the final report to our service, that is, the war crimes and genocide section.

utterances.speaker: MS. PILIPOVIC
utterances.text: Can you please tell us, since you have told us that this was submitted to your section, where are they now, I mean the shell shrapnel and tail-fin?

utterances.speaker: EDIN SULJIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: After the completion of the whole procedure, all the investigative procedures and after the submission of the criminal report or complaint, the entire case file with all the evidence is submitted to the service, where it is filed.

utterances.speaker: MS. PILIPOVIC
utterances.text: Can you please tell us where is -- where are the files or the archive, and whether the shell shrapnel are still in those files?

utterances.speaker: EDIN SULJIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: The archive or the files of the CSB, the Security Services Centre, was located in the same building where we were. At the time, it was the Blank page inserted to ensure pagination corresponds between the French and English transcripts. building called "DPO" building. Later on, the services were relocated to the same building where they were before, in the Misiribina Street, and all the documents were transferred there. I don't know what happened later and where the archive and the files are now, where all the documents and all the evidence are now.

utterances.speaker: MS. PILIPOVIC
utterances.text: Were you present at the time when the direction from which the shell had flown in was determined?

utterances.speaker: EDIN SULJIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. PILIPOVIC
utterances.text: Can you please tell us on the basis of what did the ballistics expert determine the direction from which the shell had come in?

utterances.speaker: EDIN SULJIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Both the ballistics experts and the UN representatives used the same method. The ballistics experts applied the usual methods to determine the direction from which the shell had come in, using the pendant and the compass, the rule, and -- the ruler, and perhaps some other devices. But these were the basic elements they used to determine the direction from which the shell had come in.

utterances.speaker: MS. PILIPOVIC
utterances.text: You told us that when you were drafting your final report, you spoke to the eyewitnesses.

utterances.speaker: EDIN SULJIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. PILIPOVIC
utterances.text: Can you please tell us who gave you the information that the persons that you talked to were, in fact, eyewitnesses of the incident?

utterances.speaker: EDIN SULJIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: The persons who sustained minor injuries and who reported came to the Kosevo Hospital, were interviewed about the circumstances where they were injured, at what time, and what, in fact, happened on that day at that time.

utterances.speaker: MS. PILIPOVIC
utterances.text: The persons that you spoke with who sustained minor injuries, what did they tell you at what time they were injured?

utterances.speaker: EDIN SULJIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: As far as I remember, all the persons confirmed that they were injured at the time that corresponded to the time when the projectile exploded at the Markale market, and they all confirmed that the injuries they sustained were caused by the shrapnel from the projectile that exploded at the Markale market.

utterances.speaker: MS. PILIPOVIC
utterances.text: Can you tell us what was the time?

utterances.speaker: EDIN SULJIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I think it was sometime around noon. I can't be more specific about the time.

utterances.speaker: MS. PILIPOVIC
utterances.text: You mentioned the eyewitnesses who sustained minor injuries and whom you interviewed. Can you please tell us, on the basis of what information did you contact other eyewitnesses and what did the other eyewitnesses tell you?

utterances.speaker: EDIN SULJIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: As for the eyewitnesses who sustained extremely serious injuries, we were unable to contact them at that time. But we did contact persons whom we assumed would have the information about the direction from which the projectile had come in. We conducted such interviews after receiving the report from the ballistics expert about the direction from which the projectile had come in.

utterances.speaker: MS. PILIPOVIC
utterances.text: So you confirm that after the ballistics expert determined that the shell had come in from the direction of north-east, that you went to people who lived in that part of the city and asked them whether they had heard the shell come in and at what time?

utterances.speaker: EDIN SULJIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. PILIPOVIC
utterances.text: Can you please tell us, how did you decide which people to talk to? What was the criteria? What led you to these people?

utterances.speaker: EDIN SULJIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't remember any more.

utterances.speaker: MS. PILIPOVIC
utterances.text: Can you please tell us what these people told you, what they had heard?

utterances.speaker: EDIN SULJIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: All these people -- most of these people who were in their apartments at the time or just outside their houses, they stated that they had heard at the specified time the shell being fired, the sound of the shell flying over and the explosion, which was followed by a plume of dark smoke from the location of the city centre and the Markale location, according to their testimony.

utterances.speaker: MS. PILIPOVIC
utterances.text: Can you confirm that all these people that were interviewed were, in fact, the people who are lay persons, who have never been in contact with any shells? And did they not confirm to you that they were not present when shells were fired?

utterances.speaker: EDIN SULJIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Since this was the second year of the war, all the citizens had quite a lot of experience and quite a lot of knowledge of the shells and projectiles so that these citizens, in fact, had already seen the explosions of projectiles.

utterances.speaker: MS. PILIPOVIC
utterances.text: According to you, on the basis of the sound that follows the firing of the shell, is it possible to determine the direction from which it was fired on the basis of the sound?

utterances.speaker: EDIN SULJIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: If you hear the moment of the firing and the explosion of the shell that follows later on and if you hear the sound of the projectile flying over your head, you can assume from which direction the shell had been fired, more or less. And you can see where it exploded.

utterances.speaker: MS. PILIPOVIC
utterances.text: You told us that after that, you went to the morgue.

utterances.speaker: EDIN SULJIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. PILIPOVIC
utterances.text: In your statement given to the investigators of the Office of the Prosecutor, on page 2, Document 0303-9928, last paragraph, you stated that you used the hospital register. Is that correct?

utterances.speaker: EDIN SULJIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. PILIPOVIC
utterances.text: Yesterday, in the course of the examination in chief, you stated that in the admissions section of the Kosevo Hospital, that persons were admitted to the hospital there, and that you obtained the name, the full name, the time of admission and other personal details, from there. Is the hospital registry and the book of admissions one and the same document, according to you?

utterances.speaker: EDIN SULJIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: In the admissions of the Kosevo Hospital, there is a book, a logbook, where records are kept of all the patients that have been admitted to the hospital. In the course of the procedure to determine the identity of persons who did not have any ID on them or persons who -- for whom we did not know the exact time of their admission to the hospital, we used this registry in order to determine these facts which may have been registered there.

utterances.speaker: MS. PILIPOVIC
utterances.text: Can you tell us, in the hospital registry that recorded the names and the time of the admission of the persons to the hospital, what was the time that was listed there? Because you said that this time that was recorded there made it possible for you to determine who it was that was brought in from the Markale market.

utterances.speaker: EDIN SULJIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: The time of the admission of the injured persons was approximately immediately after the explosion of the projectile at the Markale market.

utterances.speaker: MS. PILIPOVIC
utterances.text: Can you please tell us what time it was? Was it noon, 1.00, quarter to 1.00, 1.15?

utterances.speaker: EDIN SULJIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I can't be more specific about the time because I don't really remember.

utterances.speaker: MS. PILIPOVIC
utterances.text: If you told us that you had arrived at the Markale market about an hour after the explosion, in your official report, you stated that you had been notified that around 13.20, and that the on-site investigation began at 13.30.

utterances.speaker: EDIN SULJIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: As for the time frame, the times when specific activities were taken, all this is recorded in my official report, and I maintain my previous statements. But right now, I cannot be more specific because I no longer remember them exactly. I don't remember those times exactly.

utterances.speaker: MS. PILIPOVIC
utterances.text: If I tell you that your official report states that on the 5th of February, 1994, that you were notified at around 13.20, would that, according to you, be the time when you were actually notified?

utterances.speaker: EDIN SULJIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: If that is stated in the official report, then it must be the time. It is the time.

utterances.speaker: MS. PILIPOVIC
utterances.text: In relation to that point in time, 13.20, can you tell us when did the incident take place? Did you find out at a later date how much time had elapsed from the incident to the time when you were notified?

utterances.speaker: EDIN SULJIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: In my statement, in my testimony yesterday, I stated that from the incident -- from the time of notification to the time when we gathered the team, that it took us about 30 to 45 minutes. And I think that it was the time that it took us to set up the team and to go out to the scene of the incident.

utterances.speaker: MS. PILIPOVIC
utterances.text: If we take into account the time that it took you to set up the team, the team, and the time that it took you to get there, could we agree that the incident then took place after 12.00 on that day?

utterances.speaker: EDIN SULJIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: The time when the incident happened and the time that we arrived at the scene, these times are recorded in the official report. And I still abide by what I have said there.

utterances.speaker: MS. PILIPOVIC
utterances.text: So you confirm to us that the time when you were notified was, in fact, the time when the incident happened?

utterances.speaker: EDIN SULJIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MS. PILIPOVIC
utterances.text: If you were notified at 13.20, at what time, according to you, did the actual incident take place?

utterances.speaker: EDIN SULJIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: If you insist on my giving you a specific time, I would like you to give me the report because then I would be able to continue answering your questions.

utterances.speaker: MS. PILIPOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honours, the Defence can provide the witness with his official report. And since the criminal complaint also lists the time as being 12.30, I would like to -- the witness to state the actual time after being shown both the official report and the criminal complaint. Both of these documents can be shown to him.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes, please proceed. But at the same time, Ms. Pilipovic, I remind you that the witness testified that the exact times are not in his recollection any more, but in the report. So if you want him to repeat what's in the report, I mean, we can read what is in the report. But if there's any contradiction or you would like to raise any issues, please proceed.

utterances.speaker: MS. PILIPOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, I did quote the time from the official report of the witness, and now I have given the witness the criminal complaint where a different time is listed. And I would now like the witness to be quite specific as regards the time.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Could I please be given the official report, too?

utterances.speaker: MS. PILIPOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MS. PILIPOVIC
utterances.text: Mr. Suljic, since you now have both the official report and the criminal complaint, could you please tell us at what time the incident happened?

utterances.speaker: EDIN SULJIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: The incident happened at around 12.30.

utterances.speaker: MS. PILIPOVIC
utterances.text: Thank you, sir. Can you please tell us at what time you arrived in the hospital? How much time has elapsed between the incident and the time when you arrived at the hospital?

utterances.speaker: EDIN SULJIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I was in the hospital in the afternoon, after the completion of the on-site investigation.

utterances.speaker: MS. PILIPOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honours, since the witness told us that he had inspected the hospital registry and that on the basis of the data contained therein he made a record of the victims, the casualties, the Defence would now like to show the witness an extract from the protocol submitted to the Defence -- disclosed to the Defence by the Prosecution so that the witness can confirm whether this was the format that was contained in the book or the protocol that he used to take the data. I have prepared a sufficient number of copies for all of us. If this is what the witness had used, and depending on his answer, the Defence would have some additional questions for him regarding these type of documents.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Ms. Pilipovic, do you intend to tender this document in evidence? Yes. Has it been pre-numbered?

utterances.speaker: MS. PILIPOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honours, I did not mark this document because I don't know whether we want to tender it into evidence before the witness confirms whether he is familiar with this type of document at all and whether this is, in fact, the type of document that he used to note down the information about the persons admitted or brought to the Kosevo Hospital. Depending on his answer, we would then provide the number for this document.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Thank you. On the other hand, you sometimes might take the risk. If we would have to wait until the witness has testified that he knows the document or he recognises his signature, I mean, pre-numbering becomes totally impossible. Perhaps you could take the risk next time. The only thing that could happen is that it's not tendered and that the number, of course, is of no value any more. Please proceed.

utterances.speaker: MS. PILIPOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MS. PILIPOVIC
utterances.text: Mr. Suljic, do you recognise this document?

utterances.speaker: EDIN SULJIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I cannot confirm that the protocol at that time looked like this. In fact, I don't remember any more what columns there were in the protocol at that time.

utterances.speaker: MS. PILIPOVIC
utterances.text: So Mr Suljic, you cannot confirm to us that the hospital registry or the book of admissions of the Kosevo Hospital, on the basis of which you obtained your data was, in fact, in this format and that it contained this information?

utterances.speaker: EDIN SULJIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MS. PILIPOVIC
utterances.text: Witness, do you see -- on the left-hand side of this document in the lower left-hand corner, do you see the name of Stanic Zeljko?

utterances.speaker: EDIN SULJIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. PILIPOVIC
utterances.text: If I were to tell you that the Defence has a document that we were all able to see yesterday, that's the list provided to us by the Prosecution, the list of the injured persons, persons who were admitted to the Kosevo Hospital, on page 0026-8624, it's a document that's missing a page in the middle. You confirmed to us that there's a page missing. It's Prosecution Exhibit P2366. And if I told you that Stanic Zeljko is recorded here under number 112 as a person that was injured at the Markale market, would you confirm to us that you used the data here in front of you in this protocol to enter the names of the person of -- who were injured at the Markale hospital [sic] on the list?

utterances.speaker: EDIN SULJIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I cannot confirm that I used the protocol in this form to identify the persons injured at the Markale market.

utterances.speaker: MS. PILIPOVIC
utterances.text: Can you confirm whether in this hospital protocol or registry, that the time was also noted down?

utterances.speaker: EDIN SULJIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: As far as I remember, the time of the admission of the patients was noted.

utterances.speaker: MS. PILIPOVIC
utterances.text: Was the time of the scheduled surgery also noted, or just the time of the admission?

utterances.speaker: EDIN SULJIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: The actual treatment for the patient, I don't remember that item being contained in the protocol.

utterances.speaker: MS. PILIPOVIC
utterances.text: You told us today that from January 1994, you worked for the section for the investigation of war crimes and genocide.

utterances.speaker: EDIN SULJIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. PILIPOVIC
utterances.text: Can you please confirm to us when was the section established and for how long did it operate?

utterances.speaker: EDIN SULJIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't know exactly when the section was established, but in May 1995, when I left the CSB, the section was already -- was still functioning.

utterances.speaker: MS. PILIPOVIC
utterances.text: As a member, as an employee of the section for the investigation of war crimes and genocide, did you receive any reports and did you investigate any war crimes against citizens in Sarajevo committed by members of the BH army?

utterances.speaker: EDIN SULJIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: The military prosecutor's office was in charge of the personnel of the BH army and the military security service was also dealing with that, so it was not in our jurisdiction.

utterances.speaker: MS. PILIPOVIC
utterances.text: Was it in your jurisdiction to determine or to investigate war crimes against persons living in Sarajevo committed by members of paramilitary formations operating in the town of Sarajevo?

utterances.speaker: EDIN SULJIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: We had jurisdiction only over the civilians living there, and any armed military formation would not come under our jurisdiction.

utterances.speaker: MS. PILIPOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honours, if I may just consult with my colleague for a moment.

utterances.speaker: MS. PILIPOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honours, I have no further questions, and I would now like my colleague to take over.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes, please, Mr. Piletta-Zanin.

utterances.speaker: MR. PILETTA-ZANIN
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Mr. President. After consulting my colleague, we decided to hand this document as well as the following document. We would like to present this document to the witness. And there are other questions I wish to ask this witness, but before I do so, before I begin this new line of questioning, I would like to know if the Prosecution, since they have invited us to express our opinions, or they have more or less invited us to go and inspect the documents, would they be able to give us an original of one of the documents. I would like to obtain the original of 0026-8737, which is one of these documents that was handed to us in an illegible version and, yesterday, in a legible version.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Are the originals available, Mr. Stamp?

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: We have some available, and we are sending for them. I'm very happy that my friend has taken advantage of our invitation to inspect. So perhaps we could continue with his cross-examination. They have been sent for, the document that he asked for.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: So Mr. Piletta-Zanin, if it's there, it will be in the courtroom soon. Please proceed. Perhaps if you have any other subject to touch upon.

utterances.speaker: MR. PILETTA-ZANIN
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Very well. Thank you very much. We can begin by examining these famous medical documents. I would like to show the witness, Mr. Usher, please, all the medical documents such as they were tendered yesterday by the Prosecution. It's Document 3061.1, and the questions will follow.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: May I assume that you want to have the B/C/S version to be presented to the witness?

utterances.speaker: MR. PILETTA-ZANIN
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes. It basically comes to the same thing but, yes, we may show the witness the B/C/S version. And we will work together with the English text there. Regarding the document we wish to present the witness with, I believe it bears number D91.

utterances.speaker: MR. PILETTA-ZANIN
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Witness, do you recognise the documents that were shown to you just now?

utterances.speaker: EDIN SULJIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, from my personal experience, I am familiar with this kind of document.

utterances.speaker: MR. PILETTA-ZANIN
utterances.text: Very well. Witness, could you please read out loud in the Serbian language the heading of this document, or that is to say, what do we see right after the words "izvod protokola," so that the interpreters may translate that as we go along, please.

utterances.speaker: EDIN SULJIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: "Extract from the protocol of the examination/post-mortem of the dead bodies."

utterances.speaker: MR. PILETTA-ZANIN
utterances.text: Thank you. Witness, since you just told me there probably is a register of autopsies somewhere, since what you have before you is only an excerpt from that register. Is that correct?

utterances.speaker: EDIN SULJIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. PILETTA-ZANIN
utterances.text: Thank you. Witness, did you yourself see -- have you ever seen such a book, such a logbook or a register?

utterances.speaker: EDIN SULJIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I have had the occasion to see such a protocol.

utterances.speaker: MR. PILETTA-ZANIN
utterances.text: Witness, would you kindly look at the first document that we were handed, document bearing the mark 535. Do you have this document before you?

utterances.speaker: EDIN SULJIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. PILETTA-ZANIN
utterances.text: Thank you. Can you tell us, what do you read in the section "date of birth"? Is there something following the words "date of birth"?

utterances.speaker: EDIN SULJIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. It is unfilled. It is empty.

utterances.speaker: MR. PILETTA-ZANIN
utterances.text: Same thing goes for the second line where we see in the Serbian language "date of examination." Is there a date, in fact?

utterances.speaker: EDIN SULJIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, there is no date.

utterances.speaker: MR. PILETTA-ZANIN
utterances.text: Thank you. Witness, since the examination registers and the autopsy registers exist and you have seen them, could you tell us when were the autopsies carried out, on what date?

utterances.speaker: EDIN SULJIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't know which autopsies you are referring to.

utterances.speaker: MR. PILETTA-ZANIN
utterances.text: Very well, Witness. I'm referring to each of the autopsies that were undoubtedly carried out for each of the patients that are listed in the document that you have before you bearing mark P3061.1 in its translated version.

utterances.speaker: EDIN SULJIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I cannot confirm the correct date of the autopsy of the deceased citizens because some citizens died on the spot, whereas others died following the injuries. And I do not know when the autopsies were carried out on those bodies.

utterances.speaker: MR. PILETTA-ZANIN
utterances.text: Thank you. Witness, as an investigator, had you seen at the time these documents that you have before you right now?

utterances.speaker: EDIN SULJIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. PILETTA-ZANIN
utterances.text: Is it the first time you see these documents?

utterances.speaker: EDIN SULJIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. PILETTA-ZANIN
utterances.text: When had you seen these documents for the first time, please?

utterances.speaker: EDIN SULJIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I had seen these in the office of the chief of the department, on his desk. I don't recall when exactly.

utterances.speaker: MR. PILETTA-ZANIN
utterances.text: Can you tell us the year?

utterances.speaker: EDIN SULJIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I know that it was after the on-site investigation, but I do not know when exactly. However, I do know that I have had the occasion to see them once before.

utterances.speaker: MR. PILETTA-ZANIN
utterances.text: Very well.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Piletta-Zanin, could you please find a suitable moment.

utterances.speaker: MR. PILETTA-ZANIN
utterances.text: [Interpretation] This is exactly what I wanted to tell you. I believe that this is the right time to make a break. And in the meantime, I'm certain that we will receive the original of this document which will enable us to work in a precise, detailed, and sufficient way so that we can resume the cross-examination of this witness.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. Mr. Piletta-Zanin, may I also remind you as far as the time limits are concerned, as I indicated yesterday, I see that in approximately seven minutes, one hour will be used. And would you please keep that in mind. We'll adjourn until 11.00.

utterances.speaker: MR. PILETTA-ZANIN
utterances.text: Tempus fugit.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Piletta-Zanin.

utterances.speaker: MR. PILETTA-ZANIN
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. President, thank you. We all know that unfortunately, as I said earlier, tempus fugit, time flies, and I was just informed that Mr. Stamp, that the documents that I requested to obtain in their original version would be available. They are available. Mr. Stamp, would you kindly show us these documents or should we wait for these originals? Could you communicate to us the originals right now?

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: If it please you, Mr. President, Your Honours. If the document and if I am correct in saying that my friend has asked for 0026-8737, it is here. It does come from within a batch of documents. I don't know whether he wants the specific page of it or if he wants the batch. However, I could tender to him this particular page through the usher. I don't know if the Court would like to see it before.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Piletta-Zanin -- will you please show it to Mr. Piletta-Zanin.

utterances.speaker: MR. PILETTA-ZANIN
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. President, this is a perfect example of either a total misunderstanding or of something else. What I asked earlier is, clearly, is to get one of the documents --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. Let me just see whether -- it was my understanding that you were asking for 0026-8537.

utterances.speaker: MR. PILETTA-ZANIN
utterances.text: [In English] Exactly that, sir.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: What I see now, it is in the transcript, because I see that it's a totally different document. Let's just check in the transcript.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: It is, if I may assist, at page 27, line 8 to 9. It is 837 on the transcript so there might have been some error. If it is 8735, I think that is the conclusion. Because when my friend was asked for the document, we were wondering --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: It was also my understanding that it is one of these documents out of this set.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: That is what I thought. I thought I had to give the number that is required. I asked for the full set to be brought.

utterances.speaker: MR. PILETTA-ZANIN
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. President, would you please ask the Prosecution to bring us the whole set and we will choose ourselves, select ourselves.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: First, Mr. Usher, could you please return the other document to -- yes, please return it to the Prosecution, to Mr. Stamp. Do we now have -- that is 537, the last digits?

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: Here it is.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. Would you please, Mr. Usher, give it to Mr. Piletta-Zanin.

utterances.speaker: MR. PILETTA-ZANIN
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. President, I believe, having asked earlier for an original, I get one. Thank you very much for Blank page inserted to ensure pagination corresponds between the French and English transcripts. it. But this is a copy, this is not an original once again. I will work from this copy. I thank Mr. Stamp infinitely and I beg you, Mr. President, to be kind enough to be lenient towards me because if I may misread something, it will not be my fault as this document is not as legible as I would have wanted it. You see the date that is on this document, which is the date on which the post-mortem examination or, rather, the autopsy was carried out, corresponds most likely to --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Piletta-Zanin, could we just have an opportunity to have a glance at the document without your explaining in the presence of the witness all the problems that might arise from it.

utterances.speaker: MR. PILETTA-ZANIN
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Of course.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Please proceed, Mr. Piletta-Zanin.

utterances.speaker: MR. PILETTA-ZANIN
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, thank you. With your kind leniency, Mr. President, I will proceed. Thank you once again. We still do not have the original. We do have a copy, however, and I will return these documents to the Prosecution. I thank them for their kind cooperation, and now I would like to get to submit --

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: May I just say that what we had produced is the original of what we have in evidence.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: We understood that you would give it as original as it is in your hands.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Please proceed, Mr. Piletta-Zanin.

utterances.speaker: MR. PILETTA-ZANIN
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Mr. President. I would like to ask more questions, Mr. President, with regards to the document D91. This is a document comprised of a few pages and not only of one page, the page that we have tendered earlier. This is an A-3 format page that we will hand out to parties right now with the help of the usher, and these are all pages marked D91. I believe that we have a sufficient number of copies for all parties. Thank you. We are therefore talking of a document marked D91. Mr. President, Your Honours, I believe that we all have these documents for us. May I presume --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Please proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. PILETTA-ZANIN
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. PILETTA-ZANIN
utterances.text: Witness, you have before you a copy of a document comprised of a few pages. It is probably the admissions book for patients admitted in the Kosevo Hospital. Would you kindly, Witness, go to the page which at the top right-hand corner bears the number 604. Do you have this document?

utterances.speaker: EDIN SULJIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. PILETTA-ZANIN
utterances.text: Witness, do you see on this page, at the bottom of the page, on the last line which is almost in the middle of the page, under "operacija," can you see the following words: "otisao UNPROFOR - om," "went to the UNPROFOR."

utterances.speaker: EDIN SULJIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. PILETTA-ZANIN
utterances.text: Very well. I did not listen to the translation at the same time, but would you please reread this sentence so that we can understand the sentence and that it is translated so that it can go into the transcript?

utterances.speaker: EDIN SULJIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: "Went with the UNPROFOR."

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: May I just -- the line has been read now twice and the first time it was translated "went to the UNPROFOR," and second time the translation was "went with the UNPROFOR." As far as I understand it was the same words that were translated. Could the booth verify -- perhaps you spell out, Mr. Piletta-Zanin, exactly, because I do understand that the booth now has a copy. You have been literally spelling out the words that you just read and the words --

utterances.speaker: MR. PILETTA-ZANIN
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, absolutely, Mr. President. Nevertheless the sense is the same -- the meaning is the same.

utterances.speaker: MR. PILETTA-ZANIN
utterances.text: Witness, could you please slowly reread those words "otisao UNPROFOR - om" and so on, so that the interpreters may record these words for the transcript?

utterances.speaker: EDIN SULJIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: "Went with the UNPROFOR."

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Mr. President, without the rest of the sentence, it is a bit difficult. It could be very ambiguous. It is an ambiguous way because we don't know if it is the ablative, the generative, the dative.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Thank you very much for your clarification.

utterances.speaker: MR. PILETTA-ZANIN
utterances.text: [Interpretation] For the booth, there isn't anything else, and this is the question I wanted to ask the witness. There is nothing else following these two words.

utterances.speaker: MR. PILETTA-ZANIN
utterances.text: But these two words or this sentence, does that mean that the patients went either escorted by the UNPROFOR, they went to the UNPROFOR to be hospitalized there? And I am talking about the patients that went to the PTT hospital. Would that be a possibility? Can this be the case?

utterances.speaker: EDIN SULJIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I really don't know what this sentence is supposed to mean.

utterances.speaker: MR. PILETTA-ZANIN
utterances.text: Very well. Witness, were there some patients who were in such a critical state that they had to be transferred to the UNPROFOR hospital which was, if I am not mistaken, the PTT hospital?

utterances.speaker: EDIN SULJIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't know.

utterances.speaker: MR. PILETTA-ZANIN
utterances.text: Very well.

utterances.speaker: EDIN SULJIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: But I know that some patients went to the UNPROFOR hospital which was located in the PTT building.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Piletta-Zanin, may I just ask for a clarification. The translation says: "Witness, were there some patients who were in such a critical state that they had to be transferred to the UNPROFOR hospital?" It is my recollection, but I am listening at the same time to some French and to some English, was that exactly what you wanted to ask, the critical stage of the patients or...

utterances.speaker: MR. PILETTA-ZANIN
utterances.text: [Interpretation] No. In fact, the question was answered. It is not the critical state that really preoccupied me but the fact that these patients were transferred to this make-shift hospital of the UNPROFOR, and the answer was given

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: What was exactly your question? That was not clear to me. I mean, the transfer is clear --

utterances.speaker: MR. PILETTA-ZANIN
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. President, my question was -- we will see it later. Allow me just a few questions and we will see it later. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. PILETTA-ZANIN
utterances.text: Witness, please go to the next page. Do we see the same wording for the two patients or for one patient? There is also here the wording "gone with the UNPROFOR by the UNPROFOR." Is that the same wording we find on this document as well?

utterances.speaker: EDIN SULJIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. PILETTA-ZANIN
utterances.text: Witness, on this list, on this page, since we see that there are some patients that were transferred to the UNPROFOR hospital, should we not say -- and I would like to draw your attention to the stamp on the right-hand side of the document. Should we not infer, therefore, that this is the admissions book of the hospital in question, or an excerpt from the book?

utterances.speaker: EDIN SULJIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I can confirm that on the right-hand corner we see a stamp saying, "clinical centre of the University of Sarajevo, official institution," and I don't know if this is indeed the stamp of the Kosevo Hospital.

utterances.speaker: MR. PILETTA-ZANIN
utterances.text: Witness, when you carried out your investigation, you did not find any other stamps? You did not see any other stamps belonging to the Kosevo Hospital other than the one we see here?

utterances.speaker: EDIN SULJIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: When we were establishing the list of the dead and wounded, we got in contact with the people who were in charge of the protocol, and they were the ones who would give us the data stemming from the protocol that was just in front of them

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Piletta-Zanin, may I ask you something? You have drawn the attention of the witness to the entry on the bottom of the page, last three digits 604. And then you talked about another one or two patients on the second page of the document where the stamp appears. But is that another patient or is it exactly -- aren't these three entries about the same? I mean, I see no difference. If you look at the entry just above the one on the first page, you will see that it is exactly the same as the entry above. So just in order to avoid any confusion, you are talking about one patient on the first side and one or two patients at the second page. Isn't it all the same?

utterances.speaker: MR. PILETTA-ZANIN
utterances.text: [Interpretation] No, Mr. President. No. This witness stated earlier that he was not certain that this is indeed the logbook from the hospital, the Kosevo Hospital. What we would like him to confirm to us is whether this book with these new documents that he has before him has the stamp of the hospital. And I am not talking about one patient, but as a general rule, I would like to know if this is the book which refers to --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. But nevertheless I do understand what you want to ask the witness. But in your questioning, it is more or less implicated that, the second page, there is two entries and I am certainly pronouncing it wrongly, but "otisao UNPROFOR" would be about a different patient compared to the first page, the bottom of the first page. And I see from the handwriting at this moment, from the name of the patient from the entry just above it, I cannot identify that there is a second -- well, let alone a third patient involved. Of course, it is all collated. That's what we clearly see. Therefore, we found it repetitiously.

utterances.speaker: MR. PILETTA-ZANIN
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. President, I quite agree with you, but this is how we received these documents. This is what they look like. Sometimes some names are overlapping and I -- excuse me for it.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: [Previous translation continues]... You talked about another patient and I wondered whether it was not about the same patient. That is the only thing I want to be clarified. Please proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. PILETTA-ZANIN
utterances.text: [Interpretation] My distinct apologies, Mr. President. You were quite right, and I do appreciate your precision.

utterances.speaker: MR. PILETTA-ZANIN
utterances.text: Witness, I would like you to tell us, and we will see comparing with page two, the page that ends with number 604 -- I would like you to look at the left column and tell us if you can confirm as we are noticing, that there is a number in this left column, that the numbers actually follow logically from 355, going down to apparently what seems to be an increasing number. Do you notice this as well?

utterances.speaker: EDIN SULJIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. PILETTA-ZANIN
utterances.text: Can you read out loud what is the heading of this column so that we can obtain the interpretation?

utterances.speaker: EDIN SULJIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Last name, first name.

utterances.speaker: MR. PILETTA-ZANIN
utterances.text: No, no, no. That is not the one. I am talking about the column with figures, please.

utterances.speaker: EDIN SULJIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Number.

utterances.speaker: MR. PILETTA-ZANIN
utterances.text: Thank you. Witness, could you please look at the date right next to the number 355. What is that date?

utterances.speaker: MR. PILETTA-ZANIN
utterances.text: Is the time 1300 hours?

utterances.speaker: EDIN SULJIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: This is what it looks like.

utterances.speaker: MR. PILETTA-ZANIN
utterances.text: Thank you. Now, let's go to the end of this document. Please go to the last page or, actually, correction, look at the bottom of this same page.

utterances.speaker: EDIN SULJIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. PILETTA-ZANIN
utterances.text: Witness, could you please read out loud the date that appears right next to the number 383.

utterances.speaker: MR. PILETTA-ZANIN
utterances.text: What is the date appearing right after the number 382?

utterances.speaker: MR. PILETTA-ZANIN
utterances.text: And right next to the number 381?

utterances.speaker: MR. PILETTA-ZANIN
utterances.text: Witness, on how many occasions between 365 and the entry 381, how many entries do you see? If I tell you that there are 26 entries, does this seem a possibility, if you calculate and count everything?

utterances.speaker: EDIN SULJIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. If I count it, this is what it looks like.

utterances.speaker: MR. PILETTA-ZANIN
utterances.text: Very well, Witness. Let's examine now the quasi-original document bearing the mark 537, and I must tell you that I must take it into memory.

utterances.speaker: MR. PILETTA-ZANIN
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I have to memorise it, Mr. President, because I do not read it well. This is the only document that we have; therefore, I would like the usher to submit this document to the witness.

utterances.speaker: MR. PILETTA-ZANIN
utterances.text: Witness, I would like to show you this document. Witness, could you tell us, what is the date of this document? What do you see in the left-hand corner?

utterances.speaker: EDIN SULJIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: 31st of January, 1995.

utterances.speaker: MR. PILETTA-ZANIN
utterances.text: Thank you. Witness, would you please tell us, do you see under the item "date of autopsy," do you see -- under "date of examination and autopsy", do you see "date?"

utterances.speaker: EDIN SULJIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: There is something written down, but it is illegible.

utterances.speaker: MR. PILETTA-ZANIN
utterances.text: Witness, if I tell you that we can read some figures quite clearly, would you agree with me to say that we could eventually read the digits 2 and 9 and that they follow one another?

utterances.speaker: EDIN SULJIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: With regards to item 2, I cannot read what is written on this document.

utterances.speaker: MR. PILETTA-ZANIN
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. Usher, would you be kind enough to give me this document, this original.

utterances.speaker: MR. PILETTA-ZANIN
utterances.text: Witness, if I tell you that it is quite possible to read the following date, 15th of March, 1993, we read 993, would you please agree with me as regards to the year?

utterances.speaker: EDIN SULJIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I could not confirm this.

utterances.speaker: MR. PILETTA-ZANIN
utterances.text: Are you, however, able to read something, to make out something?

utterances.speaker: EDIN SULJIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Something is written down, but I cannot read what it is.

utterances.speaker: MR. PILETTA-ZANIN
utterances.text: Very well. Witness, do you know with regards to this document when -- at what date the autopsy was carried out?

utterances.speaker: EDIN SULJIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, I do not know.

utterances.speaker: MR. PILETTA-ZANIN
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. President, I think that we will ask that this original be -- Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: MR. PILETTA-ZANIN
utterances.text: Witness, is it possible that no autopsy was actually carried out on those bodies? I am talking about the medical and technical meaning of this word.

utterances.speaker: EDIN SULJIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I believe that this type of affirmation is impossible.

utterances.speaker: MR. PILETTA-ZANIN
utterances.text: Witness, you told us that you had access to the register of autopsies. Can you tell this Chamber how do you recall this register looked like from memory?

utterances.speaker: EDIN SULJIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: This logbook was carried out by Dr. Dobraca. He was the one entering the data. He had with him registers, books, that appear to look like a logbook. And he would enter the data regarding every autopsy. All the autopsies were mandatory for each dead body, and the extract of the protocol was to be handed out at the request of the next of kin or the official institution, the official institution. So all these details linked to various autopsies would be handed out from Dr. Dobraca. We would receive them through him. He would transmit these documents after the on-site investigation.

utterances.speaker: MR. PILETTA-ZANIN
utterances.text: Thank you. Witness, with regards to this register, the original register in which all the autopsies are entered, do you know from memory if the date of birth of the person that was being subjected to autopsy was entered? Do you know if the date of the autopsy and the age of the person was entered?

utterances.speaker: EDIN SULJIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't know what kind of data that kind of logbook contained. When I was carrying out my work, we would always put down and establish the identity of the people who were dead and the way they died, in a different way. But we obtained details regarding the cause of death of the person. This is what we would ask Dr. Dobraca to send us.

utterances.speaker: MR. PILETTA-ZANIN
utterances.text: Very well, Witness. But you have stated that you have yourself seen the register in question, the original register, in which all the autopsies were entered. Can you tell the Chamber, what did that book look like? Was it a big format? Is it a format that looks like this A3 format that we have reproduced, or did it appear looking differently?

utterances.speaker: EDIN SULJIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: From what I can recall --

utterances.speaker: MR. PILETTA-ZANIN
utterances.text: Yes, can you do so? Can you tell us?

utterances.speaker: EDIN SULJIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: From what I can recall, there were two, possibly three books in which Dr. Dobraca would enter the said details. They were a different format. I do not know how to describe to you the format of these books.

utterances.speaker: MR. PILETTA-ZANIN
utterances.text: You mean that each of these three books had a different format, like Russian dolls, for instance?

utterances.speaker: EDIN SULJIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Dr. Dobraca was entering the details. Under which protocol, however, I do not know. I don't know what regulations he followed. But I do know when we received the information stemming from him, we would use that documentation as a basis.

utterances.speaker: MR. PILETTA-ZANIN
utterances.text: Very well, thank you. Witness, what was the colour of these books? You may not remember the format any longer, but do you remember the colour?

utterances.speaker: EDIN SULJIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I do not remember what colour they were.

utterances.speaker: MR. PILETTA-ZANIN
utterances.text: Witness, what was the form, if you have see it? If you have seen it yourself with your own eyes, if you have seen the document, an autopsy document, what was the shape of that autopsy document? Were those forms? Was this a text that was dictated?

utterances.speaker: EDIN SULJIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, I don't remember.

utterances.speaker: MR. PILETTA-ZANIN
utterances.text: You have no memory of that, very well.

utterances.speaker: MR. PILETTA-ZANIN
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. President, I have one last question for this witness. And afterwards, I shall consult my colleague about one document.

utterances.speaker: MR. PILETTA-ZANIN
utterances.text: Witness, when you saw these excerpts that we talked about earlier, so excerpts from autopsy registers, did you notice that apparently one would systematically scratch out or modify the date on those documents?

utterances.speaker: EDIN SULJIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: What document are you talking about precisely?

utterances.speaker: MR. PILETTA-ZANIN
utterances.text: I said "systematically", which means that this was applied for all the documents that we have under our eyes and that were produced in Serbian and translated into the English language. On Serbian copies, we can see that the date was modified, it was scratched out, then a new date was entered.

utterances.speaker: EDIN SULJIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I did not participate to the drafting of those documents, therefore, I cannot tell you about them.

utterances.speaker: MR. PILETTA-ZANIN
utterances.text: No. Witness, you have stated earlier that you were able or you have seen previously these documents in the office of your superior; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: EDIN SULJIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. PILETTA-ZANIN
utterances.text: So when you saw these documents, you must have seen them in the Serbian language; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: EDIN SULJIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. PILETTA-ZANIN
utterances.text: Did you notice at the time that those documents had areas that were scratched out and that somebody tried to change the date on those documents?

utterances.speaker: EDIN SULJIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I did not have the occasion to sift through these documents. I didn't examine them. But I must -- I do remember that they were on the desk of my immediate superior.

utterances.speaker: MR. PILETTA-ZANIN
utterances.text: Witness --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Piletta-Zanin, what is it you want to establish? I think it is clear to everyone in this courtroom, especially to the Chamber, that you want to establish -- come to your point. If it is just to establish that there are entries hardly legible and other entries better legible and that they might overlap and this would require an explanation or whatever the consequences would be, if that is what you want to establish, I think there is no further need. If there is anything else you want to establish, please come to your point.

utterances.speaker: MR. PILETTA-ZANIN
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. President, you have intervened so, therefore, I will not ask the question. But if this witness had told me -- I cannot do it any more. I cannot ask him the question. But If he told me, "No I am absolutely certain that when I saw these documents and they had no traces of any scratching out," I would have asked further questions. I could have been able to ask more questions because then we would have been able to establish that at some point these documents were not scratched out and then that later the date was scratched out. But then since now we've talked about it, the witness heard our comments, these questions have no impact whatsoever. I have no further questions, Mr. President, for this witness.
