I do have one question about the way this document will be treated. I would like that the document that is before the witness, I would like that this document be filed this way, in this original format, because I personally can read the date of 1993 for the date of the autopsy, which seems to be very clear. It does not appear in any other copy, and this is why I would like to ask that this document be tendered.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Piletta-Zanin, I am aware that you did not ask the witness the question, but you also explained that it was because of my intervention that it had become totally useless. Could you tell us what question you had in mind that you did not ask the witness so that we can better assess what the Chamber should think about your complaint.

utterances.speaker: MR. PILETTA-ZANIN
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, Mr. President, of course. Gladly.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: What question would you have liked to --

utterances.speaker: MR. PILETTA-ZANIN
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I wanted to know if this witness had seen all these documents in question previously and, secondly, if after having examined all the documents on his boss's desk, would he have noticed that all of these documents were tampered with - I don't really want to use the word "tampered" - but would he have noticed that the date would have been scratched at some point or not. And I wanted to know whether if he had noticed that some passages were scratched out, whether he seen it on every document or just on some documents, and then I would have asked him if he remembered under which circumstances he was able to see these documents on his boss's desk so that we can put into time when these modifications would have occurred.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Piletta-Zanin. Then you indicated you had one last question on another subject. Let me just have a look. You said there is one question about the way this document will be treated.

utterances.speaker: MR. PILETTA-ZANIN
utterances.text: [Interpretation] No, I said that I had one other issue to deal with and it was the way this document will be dealt with, how we are going to deal with this document. I wanted to ask your Chamber to accept this document in this format because some dates are quite legible on this document only.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: That is number 537, Mr. Piletta-Zanin.

utterances.speaker: MR. PILETTA-ZANIN
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, I believe so. The date corresponds, but it is 26-8537, yes. Mr. President, I would just like to use this as an example because we could do the same thing for each of these documents and if the Defence is not doing it and not proceeding this way, it is because we wanted to be efficient and we want to save time. But what I say for this document is also equal for all the other documents coming from this set of documents. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: May I then just ask you one additional question on this issue, Mr. Piletta-Zanin. The document with the last three digits 537, am I right when it is my recollection that that is the only document of which the witness yesterday told us that this was not someone who was on the list of the deceased? I am also looking to Mr. Stamp. I don't know whether my recollection is right

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: You are quite right, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: So, of course, if you want to use this as an illustration of something, I would say autopsy reports of those supposed to have died in this shelling, I think it is the only one of which the witness clearly testified that it was not on the list of the deceased. I am just bringing it to your attention since there are a lot of other --

utterances.speaker: MR. PILETTA-ZANIN
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Very well. Mr. President, I perfectly agree with you. We are very lucky to have the originals in this room, what we call originals, in this courtroom. I would like to be able to ask another question with regards to, for instance, the document 574. We will see that the same problems occur once again.

utterances.speaker: MR. PILETTA-ZANIN
utterances.text: [Interpretation] So it's 534. It is the first document. We can go on to document 536, which is immediately after that. If I may ask Mr. Stamp --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: The Defence would like to tender for totally different reasons this document. Would you object if no further questions would be put to the witness? I mean, we can ask the witness a lot of things about this document. I do understand that it is -- the evidentiary purpose of it would be, as far as the Defence is concerned, to demonstrate that about the kind of entries we find in these documents. Of course, it would take another ten minutes to go with the witness through the document, which is perhaps not of great assistance to --

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: If it is a point that on the face of these documents that we have, there appears to be some correction to some dates --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: I disagree on that.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: Indeed. It is self evident, I think, Mr. President. You said so earlier. Blank page inserted to ensure pagination corresponds between the French and English transcripts.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Of course, it is in the transcript but there will be no evidence of this fact established between the parties of which any other Chamber, for example the Appeals Chamber, could take notice of. Would you object if -- of course, we still have to consider first of all the admission of the whole -- let me just -- in the transcript it reads that, page 48 line 10, that I disagree on that which I do not remember to have said. So we agree on that, of course. So therefore we have to consider first you are tendering the whole lot of documents and we now have, I would say, an opposing tendering the Defence first objecting against the admission into evidence for the purposes you use it and asking the admission of one document for totally other purposes, that is, to leave some visible trace of what the problems with these documents might be. Would you object against that? I would just like to know before even deliberating and considering the matter.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: If what is asked is that the Prosecution concedes or agrees that there appears to be corrections in respect of certain dates, we agree to that, on these documents, on the batch. The question of admissibility raises certain procedural and evidentiary questions. Is it a question of admissibility or a question of weight? I would submit that this is not an issue as regards to admissibility. It is an issue as regards the weight that the Court would deem fit to apply to these documents. The Court would have, of course, at the relevant time have consider how much weight --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: I do understand, Mr. Stamp. But if the Court - I'm stressing, if the Court - would not admit the lot of documents, and therefore there would be no document left in the hands of the Court and of the Registry then, and if subsequently as we heard today, Mr. Piletta-Zanin is tendering one of these documents for totally different purposes, would the Prosecution object? I would just like to know.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: We would. We would object.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: And for what reason would you object?

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: If he proposes to tender the document to prove anything which is truth of anything on that document, then we would propose to the Court that if the document can prove its contents, then similarly all of those documents could be accepted as evidence in proof of the contents. Perhaps I should rephrase it. We perhaps would not object, but we could certainly have to raise the issue as to the probative value of all of the documents, if one could be selected to say that there is some probative value in that one.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes, but I think that the Prosecution sought to have these documents admitted because of the content --

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: Indeed --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: -- of the documents. While I do understand the Defence would seek the admission of one example of it, not in order to establish whether it is true or not what's in there, but just that the document as such shows, well, let me say, multiple, partly illegible entries, and therefore is a document like the others, like at least many of the others which might have been -- at least, have been changed, altered, whatever, so that there is at least some example of what the Defence seeks to establish. Of course, that is a totally different issue. That is rather a procedural issue than a matter of content of the documents. Would the Prosecution, nevertheless, object against admitting for these evidentiary purposes, but exclusively for these evidentiary purposes, to have one example in the hands of the Court and the Registry and available to --

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: No, we would not object if one document was selected from the batch for that purpose if the Defence wanted to do that. But we would add the caveat that we still tender to the Court and ask that all be received in evidence.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Of course, it would only be -- I mean, if all the documents are admitted into evidence, 534, whatever other would be there as well. So there would be no need to decide upon the additional request from the -- or the -- I would say the subsidiary request. I think that is clear now. Yes, Mr. Piletta-Zanin.

utterances.speaker: MR. PILETTA-ZANIN
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. President, as regards to this issue, I would now like to go on --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Piletta-Zanin, perhaps it was not very wise of me to raise the issue in front of the witness. If you would submit anything that could be dealt with after the examination of the witness has been concluded, I would rather leave it.

utterances.speaker: MR. PILETTA-ZANIN
utterances.text: [Interpretation] No.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: No, okay, please proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. PILETTA-ZANIN
utterances.text: [Interpretation] No, thank you, Mr. President. We have seen perfectly legible copies, and we would like the Office of the Prosecutor to submit to us these medical reports, the autopsy reports ending with numbers 45, 46, 57, 60. Let me repeat that for the transcript: 45, 46, 57, 60, and 85, because we would like to see some other elements, such as the date, and these texts are much more legible than any of the copies that we have received so far. So could we please call upon the Office of the Prosecutor to provide us with this document in the same form that we -- that they have given us the documents number ending in number 37.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: It is not quite clear to me the numbers as ending with the numbers 45, 46, and then it is 560. I think that's --

utterances.speaker: MR. PILETTA-ZANIN
utterances.text: [Interpretation] No, no. It is always the same basis. 002685, so I am giving you just the last digits, 45, 46, 57, and 860 and 85. So I am always referring just to the last two digits.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. I think it is, then, for you, Mr. Stamp, to re-examine the witness, if there is any need to do so.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. PILETTA-ZANIN
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I have to apologise, Your Honour. I did not express myself quite clearly. What I wanted to do is in light of what has been happening here in order to make everything clear, I wanted to have these documents so that I can show them to the witness right now, so that we can see these documents that we have never been able to read them at all. We want to see them now.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: [Previous translation continues]... the documents in order to demonstrate what type of entries, multiple, double, whatever way. We went through Document 37. You want to put similar questions in respect of the ones you just --

utterances.speaker: MR. PILETTA-ZANIN
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes. Yes, for a very simple reason. You have just mentioned it yourself. The document that ends in 37 seems to be referring to one person, a person that was not killed at the Markale. So we have an interesting event here. I would like to ask a few questions pertaining to the persons who, according to the opinion of the Prosecutor, were at the Markale.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Before responding to you, Mr. Piletta-Zanin, let me first ask one question to Mr. Suljic. Mr. Suljic, you might have the feeling that you are almost lost in these procedural issues. Do you have any knowledge of the entries, especially dates, on the excerpts of the autopsy registers as they have been shown to you? Do you have any knowledge in the way the entries were made, whether they were ever changed?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I have no knowledge as to how the data was entered into these documents or if any modifications were made at any point.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Suljic. Mr. Piletta-Zanin, we have no problems to finally have one or a couple of examples of these excerpts which indicate quite clearly what the problem is so that we have, apart from on the transcript, debates or the debates between the parties and the observations of the Chamber about it. But the Chamber feels that it is not necessary, in view of the answer just given, to ask any additional questions to the witness in that respect. So, therefore, unless you indicate whether you should do it in the presence of the witness --

utterances.speaker: MR. PILETTA-ZANIN
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you. I have understood your view. But in order to be able to prepare, if we are to face the same situation again, could we again ask some questions? We would like the Prosecution to provide us with these extras that I have just mentioned, that is 45, 46, 56, 60, and 85 to enable the Defence, who will see them clearly for the first time, to even try to defend the interests of His Excellency General Galic.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Is the Prosecution willing to -- since I saw hardly any difference in the quality of the copy we just saw and the copy that had been provided to us previously, is the Prosecution willing to give, just to inspect, those numbers the Defence asked for?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: I think you missed one as a matter of fact. Let me just...

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: For the time being, we have 45, 46, 60, and 85. We will get 57. Here is 57.

utterances.speaker: MR. PILETTA-ZANIN
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you once again. Mr. President, unfortunately, I have to announce at this time that there will be some additional questions regardless of the additional questions asked by the Prosecution, because it is quite legible on this documents that the date when the accident purportedly happened is 1993, 9-3. So that would be before the February, 1994.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Could we just inspect the documents just given to you so that the Chamber can see whether there is any difference in legibility.

utterances.speaker: MR. PILETTA-ZANIN
utterances.text: [Interpretation] For us, there is one. You can see that on document 85 and on document 57.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Let me just look at these two documents. Just have a look.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: The Chamber will retire for just one moment in order to have a better opportunity than here in this courtroom to consider the matter. We will adjourn, but just for a couple of minutes. --- Break taken at 12.08 p.m.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: The Chamber has considered the matter before it. We have established that the witness, Mr. Suljic, could not authenticate the documents, the excerpts of the autopsy reports, and the Chamber decides that these documents cannot be admitted in evidence without authentication. At the same time, the Chamber would like to have for the record admitted two examples, just as a matter of demonstration of what the Defence argued as far as the entries of dates are concerned. And since the Defence indicated that 85 and 57 would be good examples, those will then be admitted at this moment. Mr. Piletta-Zanin, could you indicate whether you have any questions to Mr. Suljic on any other item, apart from the documents?

utterances.speaker: MR. PILETTA-ZANIN
utterances.text: [Interpretation] No, no further questions. I just wanted to give you, as regards to documents that you deemed to be good enough to be admitted, I would like to have them admitted. I can even turn them upside down. It wouldn't help you much because they're totally illegible, but I don't know how much use they would be to you, but I would like to have them admitted.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: I think the Chamber has paid proper attention to the fact and has expressed itself on the quality of the copies previously provided to the Defence. The Chamber has also expressed itself on the opportunity the Defence has to inspect the documents in the hands of the Prosecution, and the quality of the copies shown by the Defence is such that it would be almost impossible to detect the type of problems we now have established there are. We don't need any evidence on that and I don't think that that is in dispute since I --

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: As to the quality of the copies, we have not accepted what the Defence has said. And it was indicated that perhaps in respect of these issues we could look into our records and perhaps address the Court precisely and in full in regards to what was raised. But may I ask the Court if I can enquire and have a look at those copies that my learned friend has waived --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Could we do the following? The Defence has asked to have that admitted into evidence as well. There is no witness that has accompanied these documents themselves. If the parties would try to see what they could agree upon as far as the quality is concerned, we will not give a decision on that. We just have given a decision now on the admissibility of the documents tendered by the Prosecution, the two documents 57 and 85 that have been tendered by the Defence. Let the black box discussion first be between the two parties, and whenever it becomes relevant to the Chamber, we will find out. Yes, Madam Registrar, could I just return these documents. They come from the Prosecution. They are nevertheless tendered by the Defence, and I think for the completeness for the original files of the Prosecution, they might perhaps be first returned to the Prosecution and then perfect copies made. Yes. So if you would please first return them to the Defence. Defence will then return them to the Prosecution. That is the -- the black copies could be done out of the courtroom. Mr. Piletta-Zanin, I returned the copies to who gave them to the Chamber, but I expect that they will finally be returned to Mr. Stamp, to the Prosecution, and could you, during the break, take care that of number 85 and 57, such copies are made that best demonstrate what you wanted to demonstrate and which demonstration the Chamber has accepted.

utterances.speaker: MR. PILETTA-ZANIN
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. President, I will hand this to the lead counsel, lest the documents should be lost.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. PILETTA-ZANIN
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. President, just one more thing. I am now a victim of the blue box syndrome. I am very sorry. My computer has just given up the ghost. I hope this is just a temporary thing. I would now like to ask the technical service to provide me some assistance.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Stamp, let me first just ask you, is there any need to re-examine the witness?

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: On just one or two points. It won't be very long.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: We can do that after the break then. Mr. Piletta-Zanin, one or two questions in re-examination, would that go even without your computer functioning at this very moment, because I would like to finish the witness?

utterances.speaker: MR. PILETTA-ZANIN
utterances.text: [Interpretation] No, it is not a problem. I will be using other monitors, so if it is necessary.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: If the interpreter services, if you would agree to go on for five minutes, then we could finish this witness by now. I see some nodding.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: No problem, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Thank you very much. Mr. Usher, could you please lead the witness into the court again.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: In the interim, I'm wondering if my learned friends could let us have the batch of documents which they are complaining about, if they don't object.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: The documents --

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: The batch of medical documents --

utterances.speaker: MR. PILETTA-ZANIN
utterances.text: [Interpretation] You mean all the documents that were mentioned? All the documents mentioned in the memo dated 25 July 2001, my dear colleague, because obviously we have three pages and we don't have them here with us. It is a full complete list and you would need a cart to bring them in. So which documents specifically do you mean?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: [Previous translation continues]... This exchange of views can be done during the break between the parties. You are just filling up the moment where we were sitting idle. Yes, Mr. Usher, would you please lead in Mr. Suljic. Please be seated, Mr. Suljic. Mr. Suljic, the Defence has informed the Chamber that they had concluded their cross-examination. You will now be re-examined by counsel for the Prosecution. Mr. Stamp, please proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: You said that the register of protocol that the doctor used when he did his post-mortem, he made notes in that register or protocol?

utterances.speaker: EDIN SULJIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, Dr. Dobraca kept records of all the autopsies that were carried out.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: Those notes or records, were they done by hand? Did he write them by hand?

utterances.speaker: EDIN SULJIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I think that the records had to be kept by law, and in his register, he entered them by hand.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: Thank you. You said that the persons who were injured and taken to Kosevo Hospital suffered injuries of varying degrees of seriousness. Some serious, some not so serious. That is correct, is it?

utterances.speaker: EDIN SULJIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: And some of them would have had to have operations and some not, depending on how serious the injuries were?

utterances.speaker: EDIN SULJIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: And I take it that some of them had to have emergency operations?

utterances.speaker: EDIN SULJIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: Now, the Defence showed you a document which I think was marked D91, and it was put to you that there were approximately 26 entries between entry 354 on the first page and entry 382 on the last page.

utterances.speaker: EDIN SULJIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: Take a look at the first page of the document.

utterances.speaker: EDIN SULJIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: The last column to the right, what does that say in print at the top? Could you read it, please.

utterances.speaker: EDIN SULJIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: "Results of the surgery comment."

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: And if you count the columns from right, go to the sixth column, what does it say at the top of that column in print?

utterances.speaker: EDIN SULJIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: "Person performing surgery."

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: And in that column, there are names of doctors?

utterances.speaker: EDIN SULJIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: The column for person performing the surgery and the surgery, if you have a look at those columns on each page - I think I may lead here - would you agree with me that all those columns are filled out except in respect to the patient who was transferred to the UNPROFOR hospital?

utterances.speaker: EDIN SULJIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: And I take it that this document would reflect persons, 26 persons on whom emergency surgery was conducted?

utterances.speaker: EDIN SULJIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: And, therefore, it follows that this document would not reflect the totality of the wounded persons that were transmitted from Markale to Kosevo Hospital?

utterances.speaker: EDIN SULJIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: Meaning yes, that it would not reflect the totality?

utterances.speaker: EDIN SULJIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, this document reflects only a part of the patients that were admitted and treated.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: Thank you very much.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: I have nothing further, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Stamp. I have one question which is in addition to the questions in the re-examination of Mr. Stamp, Mr. Suljic.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Could you also read for us the third column from the left, what it says at the top.

utterances.speaker: EDIN SULJIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: "Last name, first name."

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: I am saying from the left. I meant to ask you the third column from the right.

utterances.speaker: EDIN SULJIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Anesthesiologist or person providing anesthesia."

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. And do you see that this column, with only one -- a couple of exceptions, that means as far as I can see there are only two exceptions, always indicates a name of the anesthesiologist?

utterances.speaker: EDIN SULJIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: I have no further questions. Mr. Suljic, this concludes your testimony in this Court. I know you have come a very long way from Sarajevo and we might have taken a lot of your time. It is very important that those who have been present at the time, who have been present at the place where the events took place of which the accused is charged with, that they come and testify in this Court, that they answer the questions both of the Prosecution and Defence counsel and of the Judges. So thank you very much for having come to The Hague, and I wish you a safe journey home again.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: We will adjourn until five minutes past 1.00.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: I was informed that the Prosecution would like to address the Chamber, but in closed session.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: Indeed. Indeed, we would.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Would we then -- yes, please, Mr. Stamp.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: I was wondering if we could deal with the issue of the exhibits in respect of the last witness, and then we could move on to that, if it is convenient for the Court.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Is there any relation between what you want to submit to the Court and --

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: No, there is not.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: There's no relation. Then perhaps we first deal with the documents so that it's still fresh in our minds. Madam Registrar, would you please guide us on those documents that have not yet been decided upon, to deal with those first, yes.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Exhibit P2366, list of 67 persons killed in the massacre at Markale market compiled by the CSB Sarajevo on 17 February 1994.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Piletta-Zanin.

utterances.speaker: MR. PILETTA-ZANIN
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, Mr. President. I am very happy that the Prosecution mentioned this particular document because once again, and once again I must reiterate, this document is filled with mistakes, and now I will talk about mistakes which makes our work more and more difficult. Whether this is done in a deliberate way or not, I do not know, but some of the elements are missing. They were not translated.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: One moment, please.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Piletta-Zanin, the Chamber has not noticed any questions to the witness in view of the -- of any mistakes, so -- but if you want to point out --

utterances.speaker: MR. PILETTA-ZANIN
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Gladly, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: If you want to point at concrete inconsistencies because whether there are mistakes or not, I do not know. What you might bring under our attention is whether there are any inconsistencies, you could do it now. Could you tell us how much time it would take, otherwise, we could perhaps ask you to prepare it in writing. But if you can do it briefly --

utterances.speaker: MR. PILETTA-ZANIN
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I can do it now, Mr. President, if you will. As always, I will be very brief. Mr. President, if you take --

utterances.speaker: MS. PILIPOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, I do not have the translation on channel six. I can't hear the interpretation.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Do you have the same problem, General Galic? Yes? And it is not functioning again.

utterances.speaker: MR. PILETTA-ZANIN
utterances.text: [Interpretation] It is fine, thank you. I am terribly sorry, Mr. President. Extremely briefly, if you read [B/C/S phrase], if you take the instruction that is under 623 which corresponds to the fifth page as the document appears in its order, and if you compare it to the translation which would normally appear under 7801, we can see that there is a digit mistake. We can see that number 7801 do not correspond to 623. This is undoubtedly an inversion of pages. This is only one detail. But what is really -- did you find it, Mr. President? Did you find the page and those numbers? 623 is on the fifth page. That number appears on the 5th page so fifth page from the beginning of the document. It was translated in the English language and we can read number 7801 as the last page.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: This is the same observation that was made already during the explanation. I remember that the change of pages has been -- in the translation has been discussed. 782, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. PILETTA-ZANIN
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Not only this, Mr. President, but this is no doubt an inversion of pages. But what is really worrisome here is that in the translation or, rather, in the original, and I am Blank page inserted to ensure pagination corresponds between the French and English transcripts. talking about 623, 624 and others, I can see that at the end of the sentence, at the very end of the document, at the very bottom of the page, that sentence was never translated somewhere, no matter what the order is, no matter what the number of pages that appears on the page. But I don't know what is the reason for which this sentence was never translated. The text is there, and for a change, it is quite legible. We will not accept any longer that each time the Prosecution shows us --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Could you please read what is written there. It seems to me that it might be the source or something. Could you read it in the original language or ask Ms. Pilipovic to do it.

utterances.speaker: MR. PILETTA-ZANIN
utterances.text: [Interpretation] On what page, Mr. President?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: 63, bottom line, what you were just referring to.

utterances.speaker: MR. PILETTA-ZANIN
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I will read. "CSB Sarajevo Department for Genocide and War Crimes on the day of..." And so on and so forth. The date is 17 February.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: At least it is clear what is missing, Mr. Piletta-Zanin. Is there any other inconsistency or any other objection as far as the content is concerned which would oppose against admission into evidence?

utterances.speaker: MR. PILETTA-ZANIN
utterances.text: [Interpretation] This is an objection that is a formal one; it is an important objection. The second objection is to the effect that this is a list and this list does not prove anything else other than the fact that there is a list, and this is all. So once again, these documents are incomplete, to our mind. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. Thank you, Mr. Piletta-Zanin.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: The objection against the admission to evidence of Exhibit P2366 is denied. The part of the translation lacking is not such that it should oppose against the admissibility of the evidence. As far as the probative value of the documents is concerned, the Chamber will have to establish what probative value it finally has. Madam Registrar, the next document would be?

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Exhibit P2366.1, the English translation.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes, that is admitted as well.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Exhibit P2365, report bearing ERN number 0026-8315. Exhibit P2365.1, English translation.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: They are also admitted into evidence.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Exhibit P3061, medical documentation.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes, that is as we decided is not admitted into evidence, and the same as well as for the translation that is P3061.1 [Real-time transcript read in error "P361"].

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Exhibit D91, photocopied pages from protocol book in B/C/S.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Admitted into evidence. We have not yet received the final copies to be tendered for the sole evidentiary purpose of establishing the issues in respect of the entries of dates. We will receive them, I think, soon so that we could admit them into evidence, and would you please pre-number them, Ms. Pilipovic or Mr. Piletta-Zanin. Having dealt with the documents -- yes, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. PILETTA-ZANIN
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, only for the transcript, I wanted to note that on the transcript the number is erroneously entered. It is not P361, but P3061.1.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. Yes, I see it is, yes. I found it. I see that it is a mistake in the transcript. Yes. Then we will now turn into closed session in order to given an opportunity to Mr. Ierace to bring to the attention of the Chamber what he would like. I see that we are in private session now. We are now in closed session.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes, we are in open session again. Please, Mr. Ierace, proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. IERACE
utterances.text: Mr. President, before we call the next witness, I wish to raise briefly the issue of legibility of certain documents which concerned the Trial Chamber this morning. Mr. Piletta-Zanin has handed to us two documents, which I identify by the ERN numbers. They are 0026-8585 and 0026-8537. I make the observation that legibility of documents -- I notice my friend is on his feet.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Did you want to interfere?

utterances.speaker: MR. PILETTA-ZANIN
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I am really sorry, but I have to say that the English transcript on page 66:7, what I have said in French is the following: "The truth becomes poisonous." That is what it says in the transcript. But I actually never said this. What I said is the exact opposite. I never said that the truth itself is poisonous, but that the truth that is hidden becomes poisonous. So I cannot accept that some words are put into my mouth, the words that I never said.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Piletta-Zanin, I do understand that you ask your words to be translated properly. Please proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. IERACE
utterances.text: Mr. President --

utterances.speaker: MR. PILETTA-ZANIN
utterances.text: [Interpretation] You have my limitless gratitude.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: May I take it, Mr. Piletta-Zanin, that you were referring to -- not to 66:7 but to -- well, your response to --

utterances.speaker: MR. PILETTA-ZANIN
utterances.text: [Interpretation] What I meant was page 65, line 7.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: I must have it totally different. It is my recollection where you told about the truth and the poison. Put it this way. I can't find it immediately nor or --

utterances.speaker: MR. PILETTA-ZANIN
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, that is correct.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: -- or somewhere else. Yes, Mr. Ierace, please proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. PILETTA-ZANIN
utterances.text: [Interpretation] In order for Mr. Ierace to be able to continue, since we are talking about these documents, could we please have our originals back because we don't have them any more. The Office of the Prosecutor now has our originals, and if we have to express our view, we will have to have them in our hands. These are the documents that we have just handed over to the Prosecution a moment ago.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Piletta-Zanin, it took you seven lines to ask the documents back. Could the documents be returned to Mr. Piletta-Zanin so that he can respond or, at least, when he responds. Mr. Ierace, please proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. IERACE
utterances.text: Mr. President, perhaps I will come back to that in a minute. Firstly, might I complete placing on the record the second ERN number, that's 0026-8537. Mr. President, no doubt the Trial Chamber is concerned that the legibility of documents is an issue which arises now almost daily. It is important for the Prosecution to understand thoroughly how it comes to be that certain documents are illegible. Mr. President, with that in mind, I respectfully request the Defence, through the Trial Chamber, to provide the Trial Chamber with a full and accurate explanation of how they came by the two documents which they have handed to the Prosecution. In other words, it would assist us in our internal enquiries if the Defence could indicate whether the two documents which they have handed to us are the exact same hard copies which they say they received from the Prosecution, or are they a photocopy; if so, was the photocopy made by the Defence; or are they a print-off of an electronic version of these two documents. Mr. President, when they were handed to the Prosecution, we understood that they were copies for us, and since we have had them, we have placed some pen markings on them. If my friend --

utterances.speaker: MR. PILETTA-ZANIN
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. President, I would be very happy to receive the autograph of Mr. Ierace

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Ierace, please proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. IERACE
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. President. There has been a pen mark of "35" placed on one of the documents. So Mr. President, that is my first request. My second request is that the Defence indicate with precision how many versions of these two documents they have because, as you will be aware, Mr. President, from time to time, the Prosecution has provided copies of documents on more than one occasion, for instance, initially by way of disclosure and later by way of copies of documents which are to be tendered. Therefore, I would be grateful for that. If it transpires that the two pieces of paper handed -- which were handed to the Prosecution this morning are print-offs of a CD provided by the Prosecution, then the Prosecution would be grateful to have access to that CD which we have provided to them at some previous stage so that we can make our own enquiries in relation to the legibility of these documents on that CD. Finally, Mr. President, I understand that my friend this morning complained that these two documents were typical of the legibility of the entire batch from which they came, that is, the post-mortem reports which are 0026-8533 through to 0026-8596. If my friends say that that batch of documents was given to them in hard copy form and are all in similar condition, I would be grateful to have the same explanation and to have access to those hard copies. Mr. President, I believe that if the Defence responds to this request, it will enable us to more quickly provide the Trial Chamber with an explanation on this issue of legibility. Mr. President, whilst I am on my feet, the witnesses to be called after the next two are due to leave Sarajevo this afternoon at about 3.00. I understand that the weather is very poor, unseasonably poor. In Sarajevo this afternoon, there is snow falling. It may be that those witnesses do not leave Sarajevo this afternoon, in which case, it may be that tomorrow there is a period of time when we will not have witnesses to call. We will prepare our response in relation to not only the legibility issue but also the outstanding translation issue in respect to the witnesses Trto and Kundo to be given tomorrow conveniently, if there is a lapse in the calling of witnesses. Mr. President, for that reason, I would be grateful if my learned friends could give their explanation by, or shortly after, 9.00 tomorrow morning so that we can incorporate that into our response. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Ierace. Mr. Piletta-Zanin.

utterances.speaker: MR. PILETTA-ZANIN
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. President, thank you. But the Defence will perhaps be even faster than what is required of us by the Prosecution. We will say a few things as regards to documents that we have received and the documents that I want to have back, regardless of the fact that they bear your autograph. All these documents, we received them in the form of the hard copy. So these were photocopied documents that were placed in black binders, and we received them in December 2001. This is the last version that we are using. So this is not a computer print-out because, as I have already explained to Mr. Ierace himself, that the computer system is not functioning any more. When the copies used for scanning of this data and placed on the CD are of very poor quality, the scanner does not see anything and we all fall victim to the black box syndrome. Despite the fact that we do have these assets at our disposal, we are not using them. We received this in the form of the hard copy sometime in December 2001, and I hope that now in April 2002, I hope that I will be given back the three originals that are now in the hands -- still in the hands of the Prosecution. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Piletta-Zanin. Mr. Piletta-Zanin, may I ask you one question? You earlier indicated that you received bad copies. Now I heard a -- I heard one line which makes me ask this question to you. You said the December 2001 binders, that is the last version, and you are using those. Are there any earlier versions of exactly these documents you are complaining about provided to you by the Prosecution?

utterances.speaker: MR. PILETTA-ZANIN
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I was not here, but I am told that, yes, but -- they were, but they were not of any better quality. They may have been either of the same quality or even worse. So what we requested after the year 2001, after December 2001, we keep reiterating it. It is very difficult to work on the basis of these copies. We keep on asking them please supply us with better copies. We can -- sometimes we cannot specify the document because this is a very big problem that concerns the whole of the documents. We always reiterate the same request, and we will continue to do so. Thank you very much.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Ierace.

utterances.speaker: MR. IERACE
utterances.text: Mr. President, I understand from Mr. Piletta-Zanin's response that he is saying quite clearly that the two sheets of paper which he provided to the Prosecution this morning are the exact same sheets of paper which the Prosecution provided to the Defence on the 1st of December, 2001. Unless I hear anything to the contrary, I assume that to be the case. As I understand it, the Defence was provided with hard copies of these documents, apart from on the 1st of December, 2001, on the 6th of April, 2001, and on the 8th of June in the year 2000. I would be grateful if my friends could provide to us through the Trial Chamber by 9.00 tomorrow morning their copies of these two documents from those two disclosures. This is important, Mr. President, because it is an issue which arises regularly. It is important that, in the interest of saving time, we make the relevant enquiries so that we can understand why it is that the Defence complains of legibility in some cases, where we are, at this stage, able to provide more legible versions. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: You may be aware, Mr. Ierace, that in order to prevent these incidents to happen at the trial, the Chamber has ordered the parties to complain about illegibility, at least to complain about illegibility within 24 -- within 48 hours after they receive the list of the exhibits to be used, and not to wait until we are confronted with it at trial itself. Mr. Piletta-Zanin.

utterances.speaker: MR. PILETTA-ZANIN
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, Mr. President. I have to say that I am now put against the wall by the Prosecution because I have until tomorrow morning at 9.00 to make a complaint and I don't have this material at hand. It is also possible - I don't know whether it is probable - but it is possible that the Defence has already destroyed this material. Why? We have 40.000 to 50.000 copies of hard documents. It is a whole wall of binders. If we have to keep all the double and triple copies that are illegible, then we will have to find another apartment for all these documents. It is highly possible that the first copies, the bad copies, have already been destroyed. I don't know whether it is a fact, but it is a possibility. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: We have been confronted with badly legible copies of documents. We asked for an explanation, but we did not invite the parties to spend 60 per cent of the trial time on battles on whether this document was exactly in April or in June or in December provided. If the quality of the copies that have been shown to the Prosecution and to the Chamber is a quality which has been provided by the Prosecution, even if it would be last December, and irrespective of whether at an earlier stage some better copies have been provided, I mean, they might be destroyed; Ms. Pilipovic says they are not any better. If this was the quality provided in December compared to the quality of the documents that have been presented as evidence in this Court, then there is only one conclusion possible. I am saying "if," if that is that the quality was not sufficient and that it was -- and that there were better copies available. This Chamber does not want to spend all the time to solve problems from the past, but we would like to concentrate to prevent problems in the future. That is the reason why we have ordered, if there is any problem as far as illegibility is concerned in documents, that will be tendered into evidence, that it will be reported immediately and the parties will seek to clarify the issue and, if not, the Chamber will interfere. If the parties could sit together and could see whether either to compromise or not to continue to battle on what happened 6 months ago, 8 months ago, 12 months ago, then we will not investigate thoroughly whether there has ever been a good copy or not. It is really useless to do so. Unless it is bothering the Defence at this moment, and of course we have also listened to the Defence express to be handicapped, and we try to find a solution to see what was not legible, whether there was any additional time needed, and that is the way we will approach it. But we would like to prevent this. If the parties think it is really necessary to fight the battle over the April version, June version, December version, to the bitter end, they should do it in writing. If there is any further complaint, it could be written down. It could be brought to the attention of the Chamber. It could be responded by the other party also in written form, so that we use our time in court to hear the presentation of the case and that we will spend usually the afternoons in reading how the battle between the parties in this respect develops. Of course, as soon as the fairness of the trial is at stake, we will pay proper attention to that as we always have done. But at the same time, let's solve the problems and try to refrain from digging up problems. If you want an example of that, if it would be true that these badly legible copies have been provided to the Defence in December, of course it would be very difficult for the Defence always to compare exactly to see whether these new copies are better legible or not better legible and we could start a fight on whether it was appropriate or not to destroy the earlier copies and not keep them in order to demonstrate that they were just as badly legible. I mean, that brings us nowhere. So therefore, if there is a need to fight this battle, we would rather read about it in the afternoon instead of spending our time on it in the morning. We will adjourn until tomorrow 9.00, same courtroom. And of course, unless there is some additional issue to be raised, but I look at the clock and I also look at the interpreters' booth. Mr. Ierace.

utterances.speaker: MR. IERACE
utterances.text: Mr. President, my friend has requested that the two documents he provided to us be returned immediately. I would be grateful to have the opportunity to have them overnight or at least for another hour or so, so that we can make copies of these two documents for our own inquires.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Piletta-Zanin.

utterances.speaker: MR. PILETTA-ZANIN
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. President, two things: The Defence, of course, appreciates the fact that the parity of the parties is being brought into question by this method of work; and secondly, let me answer you, I will be in a way perhaps stripped naked if I am not given back these documents that are not in the possession of the Prosecution. I will be very happy to photocopy them once they are given back to us and then provide them with the photocopies. But I do believe that it will be very good for them to return them to us now. Blank page inserted to ensure pagination corresponds between the French and English transcripts.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Would it be a suggestion that the copies will now be given to the Registry, the Registry will provide copies to Mr. Ierace and the originals will be returned to Mr. Piletta-Zanin. No other issues? Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. PILETTA-ZANIN
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Limitless gratitude.

utterances.speaker: MR. PILETTA-ZANIN
